3. It is submitted that pursuant to the public announ cement, the Applicant 
received claims from Intec Capital Limited and Employees' State Insurance 
Corporation (“ESIC”), along with a notice from the Employees' Provident 
Fund Organisation (“EPFO”) regarding alleged defaults. However, owing 
to the non-availability of the Corporate Debtor’s records, the Applicant was 
unable to verify the claims received. 
 
4. The Applicant filed the progress report  on 17.03.2022 certifying the 
constitution of the Committee of Creditors (“CoC”), wherein he 
categorically recorded the non-availability of the Corporate Debtor’s records 
and the consequent difficulty in verifying the claims received and managing 
its affairs.

convened on 25.03.2022, the Applicant was resolved to be appointed as the 
Resolution Professional (‘RP’) of the Corporate Debtor. It is further

before the Applicant, following which the Applicant re-constituted the CoC 
on 19.04.2022 and the details are as follows:

6. Applicant submits that 180 days lapsed on account of non-cooperation of the 
suspended directors. It is only after Applicant filing applications under 
Section 19 of the Code, the suspended directors had undertak en to provide 
necessary details. Based on the documents and information available, the 
Applicant prepared the Information Memorandum  on 08.01.2023  as 
required in terms of Section 29 of IBC and regulations framed therein. 
 
7. The Applicant published Form G on 21.03.2023 inviting Expression of 
Interests (‘EOIs’), in Business Standard (English) and Loksatta (Marathi) 
initially fixing 06.04.2023 as the last date  for EoI.  Subsequently, on 
06.04.2023, the Applicant received one EoI from Mr. Suyog Satish 
Pachange, o ne of the suspended directors of the Corporate Debtor. It is 
submitted that the Corporate Debtor is registered as a Small and Medium 
Enterprise (“SME”) and, therefore, in terms of Section 240A of the 
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, Mr. Suyog Satish P achange was 
eligible to submit Resolution Plan. Accordingly, Mr. Suyog Satish Pachange 
submitted Resolution Plan on 15.05.2023. 
 
8. Thereafter, the second progress report under the CIRP was filed on 
01.06.2023. The Resolution plan was placed before the CoC on 23.06.2023. 
By order dated 07.07.2023, this tribunal allowed exclusion of 180 days and 
extension of 90 days for competition of CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. Thus, 
the CIRP period stood extended to 15.11.2022. 
 
9. Thereafter, the Applicant obtained legal opinion on the Resolution Plan on 
25.08.2023. The 5 th Meeting of CoC was held on 18.09.2023, wherein 
Pravara Sahakari Bank Limited was willing to put the Resolution Plan for 
voting, but Intec Capital Limited sought time to peruse the observations 
provided by Pravara Sahkari Bank Limited, and therefore the meeting was 
adjourned for consideration of Resolution Plan.

44.  Further, Regulation 38(2)(a) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 mandates a 
resolution plan to provide for “the term of the plan and its implementation 
schedule”. The Regulation, therefore, requires the Plan to stipulate a definite 
timeline for implementation of its material obligations, so that the time 
within which such obligations are required to be performed is ascertainable 
from the Plan itself. In the present case, such an open-ended stipulation for 
upfront cash payment and subsequent payment leaves the date of payment 
indeterminate, which is in violation of Regulation 38(2)(a) of the CIRP 
Regulations, 2016.

resolution plan.

noted the defects in the resolution plan, we are conscious of the role and 
powers of the Committee of Creditors in exercising their commercial 
wisdom and that this Tribunal cannot substitute its own wisdom over such 
commercial wisdom of the CoC which has been discussed in  the case of 
Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited V . Satish Kumar 
Gupta & Ors (2019) S.C.R. 275 , wherein the Hon ’ble Supreme Court 
discussed the role of Committee of Creditors. Paragraph 31 and 39 are 
reproduced below for ease of reference:

Creditors that is to decide on whether or not to rehabilitate 
the corporate debtor by means of acceptance of a particular 
resolution plan, the provisions of the Code and the 
Regulations outline in detail the importance of setting up of 
such Committee, and leaving decisions to be made by the 
requisite majority of the members of the aforesaid Committee 
in its discretion. 
39.    xxxx Besides, the commercial wisdom of the CoC has been 
given paramount status without any judicial intervention, for

assumption that financial creditors are fully informed about

87. Section 29A(g) of the Code provides that a person shall not be eligible to 
submit a resolution plan if such person has been a promoter or has been in 
the management or control of  a corporate debtor in which a preferential 
transaction, undervalued transaction, extortionate credit transaction or 
fraudulent transaction has taken place and in respect of which an order has 
been made by the Adjudicating Authority under the Code.  
88. In view of the facts and circumstances noted in Paragraphs 76 to 79 above, 
it is evident that the Resolution Professional failed to take appropriate 
action in respect of the said transactions by examining and determination 
their real nature . If the RP had dilige ntly discharged his duties and 
succeeded in PUFE applications then the resolution applicant being 
suspended director of the CD would have been ineligible under section 
29A. To our mind it appears that no PUFE application is filed merely to 
avoid disqualification of the present Resolution Applicant under Section 
29A(g) of the Code. 
89. Therefore, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, we find that 
the Resolution Plan, as submitted, does not comply with the mandatory 
requirements of Regulations 38(1) (a) and 38(1)(b) of the CIRP 
Regulations, 2016, as it fails to expressly provide for the statutory priority 
of payments to Operational Creditors and dissenting Financial Creditors. 
Further, the subsequent correspondence and statements relied upon by the 
Resolution Applicant and the Resolution Professional cannot be treated as 
forming part of the Resolution Plan in the absence of their valid 
incorporation therein, without due process of their approval by CoC. It is 
also a clear case, where attempt has been made to prevent disqualification 
of the Resolution Applicant herein as discussed in Paragraph 76 to 8 5 
above.

90. For all the reasons discussed above, the Resolution Plan is liable to be 
rejected under Section 31(2) of IBC , and accordingly  the Resolution Plan 
submitted by Suyog Satish Pachange is rejected. 
91. The consequence of rejection of the Resolution Plan is governed by Section 
33(1)(b) of the Code. The said provision reads as follows: 
“33. Initiation of liquidation. — 
(1) Where the Adjudicating Authority— 
(a) before the expiry of the insolvency resolution process 
period or the maximum period permitted for completion of the 
corporate insolvency resolution process under section 12 or 
the fast track corporate insolvency resolution process under 
section 56, as the case m ay be, does not receive a resolution 
plan under sub-section (6) of section 30; or 
(b) rejects the resolution plan under section 31 for the 
non-compliance of the requirements specified therein,  it 
shall— 
i. pass an order requiring the corporate debtor to be liquidated 
in the manner as laid down in this Chapter; 
ii. issue a public announcement stating that the corporate 
debtor is in liquidation; and 
iii. require such order to be sent to the authority with which the 
corporate debtor is registered.”

Code, and in terms of Section 33(1)(b) of the Code, this Adjudicating 
Authority is of the considered view that the Corporate Debtor is liable to be 
liquidated in accordance with the provisions of Chapter II I of Part II of the 
Code and the applicable Regulations. Accordingly, the Corporate Debtor is 
ordered to be liquidated and the following consequential order is passed:

17. Section 33(1) provides that where the Adjudicating Authority does not 
receive a resolution plan before the expiry of the CIRP period or the 
maximum period permitted for completion of  the CIRP, it shall pass an 
order for liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. Whereas, Section 33(2) of 
the Code provides that, at any stage during the CIRP, but before the 
approval of a resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority, the CoC may, 
in exercise of its commercial wisdom, pass a resolution to liquidate the 
Corporate Debtor by a vote of not less than 66% of the voting share. Upon 
such decision being communicated by the RP to the Adjudicating 
Authority, the Adjudicating Authority is required to pass a liquidation 
order in terms of Section 33(1)(b). Thus, the existence of a CoC resolution 
with the requisite majority is the statutory precondition for initiating 
liquidation under Section 33(2) of the Code. 
 
18. In the present case, the CoC, in its 10 th Meeting held on 31.10.2025, 
resolved to initiate liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. The minutes of the 
said meeting were finalised and circulated to the sole member of the CoC, 
vide email dated 02.11.2025 . The sole financial creditor holding 100% 
voting share has approved the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. The said 
resolution satisfies the requirement of not less than 66% of the voting share 
as stipulated under Section 33(2) of the Code. The resolution was passed 
after due deliberation and in exerci se of the commercial wisdom of the 
CoC, which is not open to judicial interference. In view thereof, the

by the adjudicating authority, al l such claims, which are not 
a part of the resolution plan shall stand extinguished and no

clarificatory and declaratory in nature and therefore will be 
effective from the date on which the Code has come into effect;

owed to the Central Governme nt, any State Government or 
any local authority, if  not part of the re solution plan, shall 
stand extinguished and no proceedings in respect of such dues 
for the period prior to the da te on which the adjudicating 
authority grants its approval  under Section 31 could be 
continued.”

Resolution Applicant nor any person connected to it, as defined under the 
Code, is ineligible under Section 29A of the Code. Accordingly, the 
Resolution Plan is not in contravention of any of the provisions of Section 
29A of the Code and is in accordance with law.  
80.  In K Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank & Others (2019) 12 SCC 150, 
the Hon’ble Apex Court held that if the CoC had approved the Resolution 
Plan by requisite percent of voti ng share, then as per section 30(6) of the 
Code, it is imperative for the Resolution Professional to submit the same 
to the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT). On receipt of such a proposal, the 
Adjudicating Authority is required to satisfy itself that the Resolution Plan, 
as approved by CoC, meets the requirements specified in Section 30(2). 
The Hon’ble Apex Court further observed that the role of the NCLT is ‘no 
more and no less’. The Hon’ble Apex Court further held that the discretion 
of the Adjudicating Authority is circumscribed by Section 31 and is limited 
to scrutiny of the Resolution Plan “as approved” by the requisite percent of 
voting share of financial creditors. Even in that enquiry, the grounds on 
which the Adjudicating Authority can reject the Resol ution Plan is in 
reference to matters specified in Section 30(2) when the Resolution Plan 
does not conform to the stated requirements. 
81.  In view of the law laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court, the commercial 
wisdom of the COC is to be given paramount importa nce for approval / 
rejection of the resolution plan. As the Resolution Plan meets the 
requirements of the Code and the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 the same 
needs to be approved. Accordingly, the Resolution Plan is approved with 
the following directions:
